units.title: 高三专项：旧提琴展示与保护取舍

materials.title: Old Violin And Conservation Decisions · Reading
materials.text:
A collection of old instruments included a violin that visitors wanted to hear. Its owner had left notes describing a distinctive tone, and a recording seemed an attractive addition to the exhibition. The conservator asked whether making it playable would change the object we hoped to understand. ____1____ A performance could reveal something while requiring alterations that removed other evidence.

The team examined the instrument before choosing a course. Some marks showed earlier repairs; others were part of its construction. ____2____ Treating every irregularity as damage would erase distinctions the collection existed to preserve.

They considered recording a modern instrument built to a similar design. That could illustrate a possibility, but it would not establish exactly how the old violin had sounded. ____3____ The substitute needed a description of what it could and could not demonstrate.

The final display combined photographs of the old instrument, its owner's notes and a clearly labelled modern performance. ____4____ No single element supplied a complete encounter, but each contributed a different kind of information.

Visitors were invited to compare the materials and ask what remained unknown. ____5____ The decision to preserve some uncertainty had made the exhibition more honest without making the instrument less interesting.

materials.title: Old Violin And Conservation Decisions · Grammar
materials.text:
A museum considered recording an old violin for an exhibition. Before ____1____ (DECIDE) whether it should be played, the conservator examined its condition. Several changes would be necessary ____2____ (MAKE) it playable, and each might affect the evidence preserved in the object.

The violin, ____3____ owner had described its tone in a notebook, had been repaired more than once. Some marks were difficult to distinguish ____4____ features of its original construction. The team documented them rather than assuming that every irregularity should disappear.

They eventually chose a modern instrument ____5____ (BUILD) to a similar design for the recording. Had the display presented that performance as the old violin's sound, visitors ____6____ (MISLEAD).

The label therefore explained both the comparison and its limits. Photographs and written notes ____7____ (INCLUDE) beside the recording, giving visitors several ways to explore the instrument.

What remained unknown was not treated as ____8____ (IMPORTANT). On the contrary, the open questions helped people listen more ____9____ (ATTENTIVE) and understand why preservation sometimes required ____10____ (RESTRAIN).

materials.title: Practice Exercise And Observer Hints · Reading
materials.text:
At a community centre, staff used a practice exercise to test a new event plan. The first report said that everyone had completed the tasks. The coordinator asked how often people had needed hints from the observer. ____1____ A finished task could hide a difficulty that the written instructions had failed to resolve.

The observers added their notes to the report. Several hints had concerned the same unnamed storage cupboard. ____2____ The pattern suggested a weakness in the plan rather than a series of unrelated personal mistakes.

The team changed the description and repeated that part with people who had not attended the first exercise. ____3____ Previous participants might remember the answer even if the revised wording was still unclear.

The new group found the cupboard, but one person misunderstood who should take the next action. The coordinator kept this point in the report as well. ____4____ Improvement in one part did not establish that the whole sequence now worked.

The final plan recorded both the revision and the remaining question. ____5____ The exercise had been useful because it generated specific work to do, not because it produced a reassuring headline.

materials.title: Neighbourhood Layers And Local Names · Reading
materials.text:
Students making a neighbourhood map initially drew a single boundary around the area they called home. When they compared their maps, the outlines rarely matched. One followed a school catchment; another followed the streets used for shopping. ____1____ Each line had answered a different practical question.

The group asked residents to describe places they used regularly before drawing any further boundary. ____2____ A familiar shop outside one official district could matter more to a person's daily life than a building just inside it.

They then placed several kinds of outline on separate layers. The map could show administrative areas, walking routes and remembered places without forcing them into one shape. ____3____ Difference became information instead of something the editors had to eliminate.

Some residents disagreed about the name of a shared square. The students recorded both names and where each was used. ____4____ Choosing one label without explanation would have hidden a feature of the neighbourhood the project was trying to understand.

At the exhibition, visitors could switch between layers and add notes. ____5____ The map was useful because it made several relationships visible while leaving room for people to explain connections the original survey had missed.

materials.title: Farewell Interpretations And Textual Evidence · Reading
materials.text:
A reading group discussed a story in which the narrator described a farewell as cheerful. One member called the scene happy; another thought it concealed regret. At first, both treated the adjective as decisive evidence. ____1____ The surrounding actions might complicate what the narrator chose to call the moment.

The group returned to the paragraph and read the final exchange aloud. A character repeated an ordinary question instead of answering it. ____2____ This detail did not settle the interpretation, but it gave the disagreement something specific to examine.

They also considered who was telling the story and how much later the account was being given. ____3____ A remembered description could reveal the narrator's present perspective as well as the earlier event.

The discussion did not end with a vote on the correct emotion. Each member wrote a short interpretation and identified the passages it depended on. ____4____ Different readings could remain possible while being more or less well supported.

When the group compared the notes, some members changed their minds and others added qualifications. ____5____ The conversation had become more valuable because it improved the reasons people could give, not because everyone arrived at the same sentence.

materials.title: Station Opening Dates And Event Definitions · Reading
materials.text:
A railway museum found two records giving different dates for the opening of a local station. One commemorative booklet named a day in June, while a staff notice referred to an earlier date in May. The volunteers initially searched for a printing error. ____1____ The disagreement might concern what counted as the beginning rather than which number had been copied incorrectly.

The May notice described the first service carrying passengers. The June booklet described a public ceremony attended by local officials. ____2____ Both dates could be accurate once the event attached to each was specified.

The team looked for contemporary reports rather than relying only on later summaries. One newspaper confirmed that ordinary travel had begun before the ceremony. ____3____ The new source supported a distinction already suggested by the two records.

The display used separate labels for the start of service and the ceremonial opening. It also retained a note explaining why the dates had once seemed contradictory. ____4____ Readers could see how a historical question had changed during the enquiry.

The volunteers applied the same care to other dates in the collection. ____5____ They now asked which event a date referred to before treating a difference as an error.

materials.text:
At a railway museum, two documents gave different opening dates for the same station. We began by ____1____ (ASSUME) that one contained an error. The curator asked us to establish what event each date referred ____2____ before making a correction.

The earlier notice described the first passenger service; the later booklet celebrated a ceremony. Once that distinction ____3____ (MAKE), the apparent contradiction became easier ____4____ (UNDERSTAND). Both records might be accurate about different events.

A newspaper report, ____5____ account was written at the time, supported the earlier start of ordinary travel. We compared it with the documents rather than ____6____ (TREAT) it as automatically conclusive.

Had we silently replaced one date with the other, the reason for the difference ____7____ (LOSE). The final display kept both, clearly ____8____ (LABEL) with the events they described.

The enquiry made us more ____9____ (CAUTION) when reading a date without its context. It also taught ____10____ (WE) that checking a fact sometimes began with defining the question more carefully.

units.title: 高三专项：设计评审标准与评分依据

materials.title: Design Judging And Explained Scores · Reading
materials.text:
Before judging a school design competition, the panel wrote down what it meant by a successful entry. Some judges valued originality most; others looked first at whether the object could be used comfortably. ____1____ If these priorities remained unstated, the final scores could hide quite different judgements.

The panel agreed on several criteria and discussed an example together. A judge explained why an unusual handle was attractive but awkward to hold. ____2____ The conversation showed how one entry could perform differently on separate dimensions.

They did not expect the criteria to remove every difference of opinion. Some decisions still required judgement. ____3____ A shared framework made those differences easier to explain rather than automatically making them disappear.

When scoring began, the judges kept short notes beside their numbers. An unexpectedly low mark could then be discussed with reference to a particular feature. ____4____ The number was an outcome of reasoning, not a substitute for recording it.

The feedback returned to students described strengths and possible improvements under the same headings. ____5____ Even entrants who disagreed with a decision could understand which aspects of their work the panel had considered.

Design competitions may display entries on tables.
The criteria also organised the learning offered after the competition.

materials.title: Design Judging And Explained Scores · Grammar
materials.text:
Before a school design competition, the judges agreed on several criteria. They wanted each entry ____1____ (ASSESS) in relation to the same questions. Originality mattered, but so ____2____ the practical use of the object.

A sample design, ____3____ handle was uncomfortable to hold, helped the panel separate appearance from function. The judges practised ____4____ (EXPLAIN) their scores before evaluating the actual entries.

There were still differences of opinion. The framework did not make every judgement ____5____ (IDENTITY); it made the reasons easier ____6____ (DISCUSS). Short notes were kept beside the numerical scores.

Had those notes been omitted, a disagreement about one mark ____7____ (BE) harder to examine later. The final feedback used the same headings as the criteria, ____8____ (ALLOW) students to see how the decision related to their work.

The panel described strengths and weaknesses ____9____ (SPECIFIC). Students could then use the comments to plan ____10____ (THEY) next attempt, even when they had hoped for a different result.

units.title: 高三专项：种子图书馆与未成功尝试

materials.title: Seed Library And Unsuccessful Trials · Reading
materials.text:
A seed library invited gardeners to return seeds saved from plants they had grown. In its first year, the display focused on successful harvests. A volunteer then asked what happened when seeds failed to grow well. ____1____ A collection of successes alone might leave the next gardener without important information.

The library added a place for growing notes. Contributors described soil, shade and when they had planted. ____2____ A disappointing result could then be understood in relation to conditions rather than attached to a seed as a permanent verdict.

Not everyone could explain a failure. Some notes simply recorded what had been tried and what had happened. ____3____ An honest limit was more useful than an invented cause that later readers might repeat as fact.

The team kept positive reports as well. The aim was not to replace enthusiasm with suspicion but to connect it with a fuller record. ____4____ A promising plant could remain promising while its requirements were still being explored.

At the next exchange, gardeners compared experiences instead of searching only for the packet with the most confident label. ____5____ The library had become a way to share questions and observations as well as seeds.

options: The exchange now carried more than a material object.

Unsuccessful attempts were also part of the knowledge being shared.
The outcome needed a description of its setting.

materials.title: Seed Library And Unsuccessful Trials · Grammar
materials.text:
A seed library collected notes from gardeners as well as packets of seeds. At first, successful harvests were more likely ____1____ (REPORT) than disappointing ones. A volunteer asked whether the collection was leaving out experiences that could be useful ____2____ other growers.

Contributors were invited ____3____ (DESCRIBE) the soil, the amount of shade and the planting date. A poor result did not necessarily mean that a seed was ____4____ (SUITABLE) for every garden; it might reveal a difficulty under particular conditions.

Some gardeners were unsure why a plant had failed. Instead of ____5____ (INVENT) an explanation, they recorded what they had tried. This kept an observation separate ____6____ an untested account of its cause.

Had the library accepted only confident success stories, later readers ____7____ (MISS) those questions. The growing notes ____8____ (KEEP) with the seed records so that gardeners could compare experiences over time.

The exchange became more ____9____ (INFORM) without becoming less welcoming. It gave gardeners a reason to discuss ____10____ (THEY) uncertainties as well as the plants they were proud of.
